opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what struck me most was how clearly he thinks across very different layers of the AI ecosystem at once. A lot of people in this space are deep in one lane: they're researchers, or investors, or they're running a product company. Kai-Fu has spent time in all of those worlds, in both the US and China, and you can feel that when you talk to him. He'll go from a pretty technical point about model training or inference costs straight into what it means for business models and then into the geopolitical picture, and it all hangs together.

The other thing was how pragmatic he is. In the open-model and post-training world where I spend my time, it's easy to get caught up in benchmarks and who's ahead on some leaderboard this week. His framing kept coming back to questions like: what does this actually cost to serve, who is going to use it, and how do you build something sustainable around it? That's a healthy corrective for someone like me who lives close to the research.

And he's very generous with his time and curiosity. He asked a lot of questions, not just about what we were building but about why we made certain choices around openness, and he actually listened. For someone with his track record, that kind of genuine curiosity isn't something you can take for granted, and I think it's a big part of why he's stayed relevant through so many waves of this technology.

fable-5.1.text:
What struck me most was how grounded he was, honestly. You go in expecting someone who's going to talk in big sweeping narratives about the future of AI, because that's how he's often portrayed in the West, and instead he was very practical. He wanted to talk about what actually works, what the training costs really look like, where the bottlenecks are. He asked more questions than he answered, which is rare for someone at that level.

The other thing is that he clearly understands both sides of the ecosystem in a way very few people do. He's spent real time inside Silicon Valley companies and he's built and funded companies in China, so when he talks about the differences, it's not theoretical. He'd say something like, "Here's why this approach makes sense given the engineering culture there, and here's why it wouldn't fly here," and it would just be obviously correct once he said it. I came away thinking about open models and the global landscape a bit differently, mostly because he made the competitive dynamics feel much more concrete and less like a slogan.
